sops.title: SOP for Sustainable Product Use and End-of-Life Measures for Arrival Fashion Ltd.

blocks.text: The purpose of this Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) is to establish guidelines and practices for minimizing the environmental impacts of products manufactured by Arrival Fashion Ltd. throughout their lifecycle. This SOP covers product use measures and end-of-life management, ensuring that products are used efficiently and responsibly, and that their disposal or recycling supports sustainability and minimizes environmental harm.

This SOP applies to all employees, contractors, and third-party associates involved in the design, development, distribution, use, and end-of-life management of garments produced by Arrival Fashion Ltd. body.text: Product Use Phase:

substeps.text: Environmental Impact Studies: Arrival Fashion Ltd. conducts detailed studies to assess the environmental impacts of garments during their use phase. These studies focus on common environmental impact categories such as climate change (global warming potential), acidification, eutrophication, ozone depletion, photochemical smog formation, particulate matter, ecotoxicity, and resource depletion.

Best Practices for Product Use: The company provides users with information on best practices for garment care, enabling them to minimize resources such as water and energy during use. For example, recommendations for washing garments in cold water, line drying, and proper garment maintenance are shared with consumers to extend the lifespan of the products.

Design for Resource Efficiency: Garments are designed to consume fewer resources during their use. Examples include energy-efficient manufacturing techniques and water-saving designs (e.g., fabrics that dry quickly or require less water during washing). Additionally, products are designed to minimize the need for consumable items such as detergents or fabric softeners.

Microfiber Release Prevention: Arrival Fashion Ltd. implements improved fiber treatments and garment designs to minimize the release of microfiber particles during washing. The company explores sustainable fabric technologies to reduce microfiber pollution in the environment, particularly during garment care.

body.text: End-of-Life Management:

substeps.text: Collaboration for Product Recovery: Arrival Fashion Ltd. collaborates with external parties such as Producer Responsibility Organizations (PROs), environmental NGOs, and industry coalitions to help consumers manage garments at their end-of-life. This collaboration supports initiatives for product recovery, recycling, and proper disposal.

User Information for Disposal: Information is provided to consumers on how to return, recycle, or dispose of garments responsibly. This includes details about local recycling programs, drop-off locations, and ways to repurpose or donate old garments to reduce landfill waste. The company emphasizes recycling programs aimed at minimizing waste and using less virgin material in the creation of new products.

Packaging Optimization: Arrival Fashion Ltd. focuses on reducing the environmental footprint of garment packaging. The company uses lightweight, recyclable, and monomaterial packaging to facilitate easier disposal or recycling by the consumer. Packaging is designed to minimize excess material and support efficient waste management.

Design for Recycling and Reuse: Garments are designed to be disassembled and recycled at their end-of-life. This includes using recyclable materials, modular designs, and avoiding non-recyclable components such as excessive use of synthetic adhesives, buttons, or zippers that could hinder the recycling process.

Product Collection Scheme: Arrival Fashion Ltd. has implemented a product collection scheme allowing customers to return worn garments for recycling or remanufacturing. This scheme is free of charge and ensures that garments are either remanufactured into new products, broken down for material recycling, or disposed of in an environmentally responsible manner.

sops.title: SOP for Minimizing VOC Emissions from Finished Products to Prevent Customer Health Hazards

blocks.text: This Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) defines the systematic approach for minimizing volatile organic compound (VOC) emissions from finished garments manufactured by Arrival Fashion Ltd. The primary aim is to protect customer health by preventing sensory irritation symptoms (such as eye, nose, and throat irritation, headaches, and respiratory discomfort) that may arise from residual VOCs in new garments, while ensuring compliance with international safety standards and enhancing customer confidence in product safety.

This procedure applies to all employees, contractors, suppliers, and third-party associates involved in product design, material sourcing, chemical procurement, production, quality assurance, and finished product release at Arrival Fashion Ltd. It covers the entire product lifecycle from raw material selection to finished garment dispatch, focusing on VOC control in dyes, pigments, printing pastes, finishing agents, adhesives, and other chemical inputs.

steps.heading: Regulatory Framework and Industry Standards Compliance

body.text: Regulatory Framework and Industry Standards Compliance

substeps.text: OEKO-TEX STANDARD 100 Compliance: All finished garments intended for direct customer contact must comply with OEKO-TEX STANDARD 100 certification requirements. As of the 2025 standard update, VOC parameters have been formally included in Appendix 4 of the testing scope to ensure final consumer health protection. AFL requires compliance with the following VOC limits:

ZDHC Manufacturing Restricted Substances List (MRSL) Alignment: AFL requires all chemical suppliers to demonstrate ZDHC MRSL conformance (minimum Level 1) for all dyes, printing pastes, finishing agents, and cleaning solvents used in production. The ZDHC MRSL prohibits intentional use of high-VOC chemical formulations in textile processing facilities.

Bangladesh Legal Compliance: All VOC control measures comply with the Bangladesh Labour Act, 2006 (Chapter VII on Health, Hygiene and Safety) and the Bangladesh Environment Conservation Act, 1995 as amended.

body.text: Low-VOC Material Sourcing and Procurement

substeps.text: Certified Low-VOC Input Materials: The Procurement Department shall prioritize sourcing of the following low-VOC or VOC-free materials: Water-based pigments and printing pastes instead of solvent-based formulations; Low-VOC or formaldehyde-free finishing agents (softeners, easy-care finishes, water repellents); Water-based PU coatings instead of solvent-based PU for functional finishes; Low-VOC cleaning solvents for screen preparation and equipment maintenance; Water-based adhesives for bonding and lamination processes

Supplier Certification Requirements: All chemical and dye suppliers must provide: Valid OEKO-TEX ECO PASSPORT certification or ZDHC MRSL conformance certificate (Level 1 or above); Safety Data Sheets (SDS) with VOC content disclosure; Third-party VOC test reports for each supplied batch; Declaration of conformity with AFL's Restricted Substances List (RSL)

Incoming Chemical Inspection: Upon receipt of all chemical shipments, the Quality Assurance team shall: Verify supplier certificates and SDS documentation; Conduct random VOC screening tests on high-risk chemical categories (printing pastes, finishing agents, adhesives); Reject and return any shipment that exceeds AFL's VOC acceptance criteria; Maintain records of all incoming chemical inspections for audit purposes

steps.heading: Production Process Optimization to Minimize VOC Residue

body.text: Production Process Optimization to Minimize VOC Residue

substeps.text: Application Control: The Production team shall ensure that chemical application processes are optimized to minimize VOC residues: Use closed-loop dispensing systems for volatile chemicals to reduce atmospheric release; Install local exhaust ventilation (LEV) systems in screen preparation, printing, and finishing areas; Implement automated dosing systems for dyeing and finishing operations; Apply precise application quantity controls to avoid over-application

Temperature and Curing Optimization: To ensure complete VOC volatilization during production (not residual in finished product): Maintain curing temperatures within manufacturer-specified ranges (typically 140°C to 170°C for fixation); Monitor conveyor speeds and dwell times to ensure adequate heat exposure; Calibrate curing ovens and heat-setting machines monthly; Document curing parameters for each production batch

Drying Process Control: Use controlled drying conditions with adequate airflow and temperature; Avoid under-drying which may trap VOCs within the fabric matrix; Avoid over-drying which may degrade fabric and cause VOC off-gassing from thermal decomposition

Aeration and Degassing: For finished garments with potential residual VOC content (e.g., printed, coated, or heavily finished products): Allow minimum 24 hours of aeration in well-ventilated storage before packing; For high-risk products, use forced air circulation in finished goods holding area; Consider accelerated degassing using warm air (40°C) circulation for 4–6 hours

steps.heading: Finished Product VOC Verification and Testing

body.text: Finished Product VOC Verification and Testing

substeps.text: Routine Product Testing: The Quality Assurance Department shall conduct VOC testing on finished garments according to the following schedule

Third-Party Certification: AFL maintains OEKO-TEX STANDARD 100 certification for all product categories. The certification process includes: Annual renewal testing by OEKO-TEX approved laboratories; Testing of all components including fabric, trims, buttons, zippers, labels, and threads; Compliance with current VOC limits as specified in the OEKO-TEX STANDARD 100 standard (VOC parameter effective from January 1, 2025 after transition period)

ZDHC Air Emissions Module Compliance: For facilities with wet processing or chemical-intensive operations, AFL uses the ZDHC Air Emissions Module to calculate Potential to Emit (PTE) VOC values using existing chemical inventory and SDS data, supporting performance benchmarking and targeted substitution of high-VOC chemicals.

Sensory Odor Assessment: In addition to analytical testing, all finished garments undergo sensory odor assessment by trained Quality Assurance personnel: Test conducted upon opening of packed finished goods; Assess for sharp, chemical, or irritating odors; Any garment with detectable irritating odor is quarantined for analytical testing; Products failing sensory assessment are reprocessed (re-aerated or re-washed) or rejected

body.text: Customer Communication and Transparency

substeps.text: OEKO-TEX Labeling: All OEKO-TEX STANDARD 100 certified products shall display the OEKO-TEX label with certificate number prominently on product packaging or hang tags, providing customers with visible assurance of low-VOC and safety compliance.

Low-VOC Product Brochure / Communication: AFL maintains product literature and digital content communicating its low-VOC commitment. This includes: Product brochures stating VOC-controlled manufacturing and OEKO-TEX certification; Sustainability reports detailing VOC reduction initiatives and achievements; Customer-facing information on garment care to preserve low-VOC properties (e.g., cold wash, air dry recommendations)

Customer Inquiry Response: Customer service representatives shall be trained to respond to customer inquiries regarding product VOC safety, chemical management, and certification status, providing test reports upon request where confidentiality agreements permit.

kpis.indicator: VOC test results (pass/fail rates, VOC levels by product category, trends)

narrative.text:
VOC Testing Dashboard: The Quality Assurance team maintains a monthly dashboard tracking all VOC test results, including pass/fail rates, VOC levels by product category, and trends over time.
Supplier Performance Monitoring: The Procurement Department monitors supplier VOC compliance quarterly. Suppliers with repeated non-compliance are placed on corrective action or removed from approved supplier list.
Annual Procedure Review: This SOP will be reviewed annually by the Quality Assurance Manager and Sustainability Officer to incorporate any changes in regulatory requirements (e.g., REACH updates), industry standards (OEKO-TEX, ZDHC updates), or company practices.

blocks.text:
Regulatory Adherence: All products must comply with applicable national and international regulations including OEKO-TEX STANDARD 100, REACH Regulation (EC) No 1907/2006, AFIRM RSL, and Bangladesh Environment Conservation Act 1995 regarding chemical safety.
Non-Compliance Handling: Any finished product batch failing VOC limits will be quarantined immediately. The batch may be reprocessed (re-washed and re-aerated) or rejected. Root cause analysis will identify the source (material, process, chemical), and corrective actions will be implemented.
Reporting: Any customer complaint related to product odor or respiratory irritation shall be immediately investigated by the Quality Assurance and Compliance teams, with findings reported to senior management.

sops.title: SOP for Third Party Due Dilligence

blocks.text: This Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) establishes a structured due diligence framework for investigating all third parties that Arrival Fashion Ltd engages with, including suppliers, vendors, commission agents, brokers, sales representatives, distributors, contractors, customs brokers, and consultants. The primary aim is to prevent third-party corruption incidents and ensure compliance with anti-corruption laws (e.g., Bangladesh Corruption Prevention Act, UK Bribery Act, US FCPA) and information security standards, thereby protecting the company’s reputation, assets, and legal standing.

This procedure applies to all employees, managers, and departments involved in onboarding, contracting, or renewing relationships with third parties that act on behalf of or provide services to Arrival Fashion Ltd. It covers all third parties regardless of geography, with enhanced scrutiny for high-risk categories (e.g., agents, brokers, consultants, customs brokers). Existing third-party relationships must be re-evaluated under this SOP within 12 months of its effective date.

steps.heading: Risk-Based Approach to Third-Party Due Diligence

body.text: All third parties shall be categorized into three risk tiers based on the following criteria:

rows: Operates in high-corruption-perception countries (CPI score below 50); involves government interaction; handles company funds; has access to sensitive information; provides services without fixed assets
Customs brokers, commission agents, consultants, distributors in high-risk jurisdictions
Operates in moderate-risk countries; has limited government interaction; handles non-sensitive data; established reputation
Regional suppliers, contractors, sales representatives in stable markets
Operates in low-corruption-perception countries (CPI score above 70); no government interaction; publicly listed or well-known entities; limited data access
Large fabric mills, trim suppliers, logistics providers in OECD countries

substeps.text: Country Risk Assessment: AFL maintains a country risk matrix updated annually based on Transparency International’s Corruption Perceptions Index (CPI) and the Basel AML Index. Third parties headquartered or operating in countries with: CPI score below 50 → Automatic High Risk; CPI score 50–69 → Medium Risk (unless other factors increase risk); CPI score 70+ → Low Risk (subject to other red flags)

Transaction-Based Risk Factors: Additional risk factors that may elevate a third party’s risk tier regardless of country classification: Request for unusual payment terms (e.g., cash payments, payments to third-country bank accounts); Request for payments to be made to a different legal entity than the contracting party; Unusually high commissions or success fees (above industry norm of 5-10%); Lack of physical office, website, or verifiable business presence; Reluctance to provide ownership or beneficial ownership information; Previous allegations or convictions for corruption or security breaches

Periodic Reassessment: Third-party risk tiers shall be reassessed annually or upon any significant change in the relationship (e.g., new contract, change in ownership, expansion into new geography). A third party may be moved to a higher or lower tier based on updated information.

steps.heading: Collection of Data on Third Parties

substeps.text: Third-Party Due Diligence Questionnaire (DDQ): All third parties, regardless of risk tier, must complete the AFL Third-Party Due Diligence Questionnaire. The questionnaire collects Section A – Entity Information; Section B – Ownership and Control; Section C – Anti-Corruption Compliance; Section D – Information Security Compliance; Section E – Financial and Operational (as detailed in the source questionnaire)
Supporting Documentation Collection: The following documents must be collected and verified for each third party based on risk tier (see table below)

Independent Verification: For high-risk third parties, the Compliance Officer shall conduct independent verification of collected data using commercial databases, government registers, sanctions lists, adverse media searches, and social media and professional network profiles

Data Retention: All collected third-party data shall be stored in a secure, access-restricted due diligence database. Records shall be retained for the duration of the business relationship plus seven years after termination.

body.text: Internal Benchmarking Against AFL Standards: Each third party’s responses shall be benchmarked against AFL’s internal anti-corruption and information security standards using the scoring matrix below. A third party scoring below the passing threshold in any category shall be subject to enhanced due diligence or rejection.

substeps.text: External Benchmarking Against Industry Peers: For medium and high-risk third parties, the Compliance Officer shall benchmark the third party against industry peers using industry association membership and standing; third-party ratings (e.g., EcoVadis for sustainability, which includes ethics); customer feedback and public reviews; and comparison of commission rates, fees, or pricing against market averages (significant deviations require explanation).

Due Diligence Outcome Categories: Based on the collected data and benchmarking results, each third party receives one of the following outcomes: Approved; Approved with Conditions; Further Review Required; Rejected (see table below)

Submission: The business owner (e.g., Procurement Manager, Sales Manager, Production Manager) initiates due diligence by submitting the completed Third-Party Due Diligence Questionnaire and supporting documents to the Compliance Officer.

Initial Screening: The Compliance Officer conducts sanctions and adverse media screening within 3 business days. Any positive hit on sanctions or serious corruption allegations triggers immediate escalation to the Head of Compliance and Legal.

Full Due Diligence: For low and medium-risk third parties, full due diligence (including questionnaire review, document verification, reference checks) shall be completed within 10 business days. For high-risk third parties, enhanced due diligence (including independent verification and benchmarking) shall be completed within 20 business days.
Approval Levels: Low Risk – Compliance Officer; Medium Risk – Head of Compliance; High Risk – Head of Compliance + Ethics Committee

Contractual Safeguards: All approved third parties shall execute a contract containing the following clauses: Anti-corruption representation and warranty; Right to audit (books, records, facilities) for anti-corruption and information security compliance; Information security and data protection obligations; Termination for cause upon any violation; Subcontracting approval requirement

Annual Re-Certification: All third parties shall complete an annual re-certification questionnaire. Any material changes (e.g., ownership change, new government contracts) must be reported within 30 days.
Continuous Monitoring: High-risk third parties shall be subject to continuous sanctions and adverse media monitoring using automated tools. Alerts shall be investigated within 5 business days.

Trigger-Based Re-Due Diligence: Full due diligence shall be re-initiated upon change in ownership (>25%); new country of operation (especially high-risk jurisdictions); significant adverse media report; or request for contract amendment involving payments, commissions, or data access

narrative.text:
Quarterly Due Diligence Dashboard: The Compliance Officer shall prepare a quarterly dashboard showing: number of third parties vetted, risk tier distribution, outcomes (approved, conditional, rejected), and any red flags identified.
Annual Procedure Review: This SOP shall be reviewed annually by the Head of Compliance to incorporate changes in anti-corruption laws (e.g., updates to Bangladesh anti-corruption statutes, international standards) and information security regulations (e.g., GDPR, local data protection laws).

blocks.text:
Mandatory Compliance: No third party shall be engaged without completion of the due diligence process and approval per the approval matrix. Any employee who knowingly engages an unvetted third party may face disciplinary action up to and including termination.
Reporting Violations: Any suspected corruption or security breach involving a third party must be reported immediately to the Compliance Officer or through the whistleblower channel. Retaliation against reporters is strictly prohibited.
Record Retention: All due diligence records (questionnaires, supporting documents, approval emails, monitoring alerts) shall be retained for the duration of the relationship plus seven years.

blocks.text: This SOP will be reviewed annually by the Head of Compliance and the Ethics Committee to ensure alignment with evolving anti-corruption laws (e.g., updates to Bangladesh’s Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 as amended) and information security standards (e.g., ISO 27001 updates, new data protection regulations). Updates will be communicated to all relevant departments through training sessions and documented procedure revisions.
